# The Cost of Intelligence, Episode 20: Two AI Price Cliffs Are Coming


### Gemini 4 Argon doubles December 1 and GPT-5.6 Sol’s promo ends November 30. Plus GPU rents, CoreWeave’s $47B of debt, an OpenRouter leak, and three cost cuts.


[Strong Compute](https://substack.com/@strongcompute)


Nov 23, 2026


*Listen to this episode on [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/4iRMn7193JAUGrCtyrySiL) or watch it on [YouTube](https://youtu.be/1wMYEshk4lY) .*


Welcome back to


**The Cost of Intelligence** , our comedy news show about the money behind AI. Each episode, Ben Sand reads the industry’s invoice and asks one question: are you getting more intelligence per dollar?


This week:


**Markup Monday** checks the GPU rent.


**Two AI price cliffs** land next week, on Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol.


**CoreWeave’s** bank statement.


**OpenRouter** removes three providers after a security firm’s fake secrets leaked. Plus three cuts from the Department of Token Efficiency. Black Friday is this week, and the labs are running it in reverse. Here’s the written version, with every source linked.


---


## Markup Monday


Tokens come from models. Models need an office, and that’s where our landlords, the clouds, come in.


**H100.** On Ornn’s index of actual rentals, an Nvidia H100 settled at


**$2.89 an hour** on Saturday (


[Ornn](https://data.ornn.com/markets/h100-sxm) ). That’s down about


**9%** on the week (from $3.19) and


**7%** on the month. It ends


**five straight weeks** of rising rent, from $2.65 on October 10 to $3.19 on November 14.


**B200.** The newer B200 settled at just over


**$9 an hour** ($9.09), down about


**6%** on the week and


**3%** on the month (


[Ornn](https://data.ornn.com/markets/b200) ).


Over three months, the H100 is back where it started in August ($2.90). The B200 is still about


**38%** higher than August’s $6.60. One B200 hour costs about three H100 hours. That’s the corner office, at three cubicles’ rent.


**B300.** The newest chip is on a different index, from Liquid Compute:


**$7.21 an hour** on November 17, down about


**5%** on the month (


[Liquid Compute](https://liquidcompute.com/share/b300-20261117-KkdYez2XfX8ink5A/1m-card) ). Ronit Jain, whose firm runs that index, expects the price to keep falling: “I would expect B300 pricing to continue declining” (


[Ronit Jain on X](https://x.com/ronitrjain/status/2123212182070370587) ).


**Crusoe** is going the other way. On December 1, its on-demand B300 list price goes from $8.96 to


**$9.90 an hour** , about


**10%** more (


[Crusoe](https://www.crusoe.ai/cloud/pricing) ). An index shows what renters paid. A list price shows what the landlord would like.


**The landlords’ own rent.** After Friday’s selloff, CoreWeave closed at


**$39.51** , down


**12%** on the day and about


**71%** below its 52-week high of $138.25, set in May (


[CNBC market data](https://www.cnbc.com/quotes/CRWV) ; our arithmetic). That’s more than H100 rent fell all week.


The vibe this week: tenants got a break. Landlords got the bill.


---


## Two price cliffs


**Gemini 4 Argon.** On Tuesday, December 1, Google’s API price for Argon doubles, from $2 to


**$4** per million input tokens and from $10 to


**$20** per million output tokens (


[Google AI Studio pricing](https://aistudio.google.com/docs/pricing) ). Today, ten dollars buys a million output tokens. After December 1, you’ll need to pony up twenty.


**GPT-5.6 Sol.** OpenAI’s promo price,


**$4 in and $20 out** per million tokens, runs until


**November 30** (


[OpenAI](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/models/gpt-5.6-sol) ). So today, twenty dollars buys a million Sol output tokens: what Argon will buy after December 1. After the promo, Sol goes back to its regular price. OpenAI’s model page doesn’t list it; the discounts it describes (20% off input, 33% off output) would put it around $5 in and $30 out (our arithmetic).


Every promo price comes with a second price. It’s called December.


*Per-dollar verdict: the cheap prices end next week. Budget for the list price.*


---


## The landlord’s bank statement


CoreWeave is one of those landlords. It borrowed heavily to buy its GPUs.


-


Its debt was


**$46.9 billion** at the end of September, up from


**$35.1 billion** three months earlier: about a third more in one quarter (


[CoreWeave Q3 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000461/coreweave3q26earningspress.htm) ;


[Q2 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000362/coreweave2q26earningspress.htm) ).


-


About


**$11 billion** of principal comes due in 2027, per its quarterly filing (


[10-Q](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000465/crwv-20260930.htm) ). The Guardian reported more than $10 billion due next year.


-


CoreWeave expects interest expense of


**$1.05 to $1.15 billion** this quarter. Last quarter, net interest of $846 million took about


**23%** of its $3.66 billion revenue (


[CoreWeave Q3 results](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1769628/000176962826000461/coreweave3q26earningspress.htm) ; our arithmetic).


The chips run hot. The interest runs hotter.


And Nvidia’s own filing lists


**$32 billion** of future commitments to neoclouds, the GPU rental clouds like CoreWeave. They take effect only if the neoclouds secure financing, and the capacity is deployed, made operational and accepted by Nvidia (


[Nvidia CFO commentary](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1045810/000104581026000088/q3fy27cfocommentary.htm) ). Even the GPUs work for the bank now.


*Per-dollar verdict: the landlord’s loan payment is baked into your rent, even in a week the rent fell.*


---


## A leak


OpenRouter is a marketplace. It sends your request to whichever company hosts the model, often the cheapest. Think of it as a food court for models.


On Sunday, OpenRouter said it had removed


**three providers** and pulled


**125 endpoints** off its zero data retention list, for customers who never want their prompts kept. It says it was not breached, and it doesn’t name the three (


[OpenRouter](https://openrouter.ai/blog/announcements/data-processing-incidents-on-inference-providers/) ).


The trigger was a study by the security firm


**Dragos** . From July to November it planted fake secrets in nearly


**two million** prompts, then watched who touched them. It says data from at least


**three** providers was exposed (


[Dragos](https://www.dragos.com/blog/ai-supply-chain-security-canary-tokens) ).


One host did post a confession.


**Together AI** says an AI coding agent leaked a credential, and someone downloaded samples of old prompts from June and July. Five of the credentials tested were Dragos’s fakes (


[Together AI](https://www.together.ai/blog/security-event-prompt-leakage-for-requests-in-june-and-july-of-2026) ). Together AI doesn’t say it was one of the three providers OpenRouter removed.


Zero data retention turned out to be a mission statement.


*Per-dollar verdict: a cheap token that leaks costs more than a pricey one that doesn’t.*


All that to drive a future filled with


**Slipping Intelligence** , or SI for short. The rent slips. The price list doesn’t.


---


## Department of Token Efficiency


Chainsaw fueled. Receipts out.


**Cut one: Value Added Tech stopped mailing the manuals.** Value Added Tech is a consulting and automation firm. Its coding agents sent


**178** tool descriptions with every request, about half of each request (


[Value Added Tech](https://vatech.io/blog/llm-cost-optimization-litellm-opencode/) ). The agent was carrying the whole IKEA catalog to buy one Allen key.


So they swapped most of the manuals for a searchable tool catalog, with three tools: search, describe and call. The agent looks up a tool when it needs one, and tools per request fell from 178 to 28. Which is how every human builds IKEA furniture.


In a week, cost per request fell about


**74%** (from about 6.7 cents to 1.8 cents), weekly spending fell by more than a third (from $879 to $561), and they ran about


**2.45x** the requests.


**The fine print:** it’s one consulting firm’s blog post, one week after the change. Requests rose on purpose, so cost per request and total spend tell different stories.


**Cut two: OpenCode’s sale, with no announced end date.** OpenCode is a coding tool that hosts free-weights models. On Saturday it cut the price of two of them by


**60%** (


[OpenCode PR #65470](https://github.com/anomalyco/opencode/pull/65470) ):


-


**GLM 5.3** : $1.40 / $4.40 to


**$0.56 / $1.76** per million input / output tokens.


-


**DeepSeek V4.1 Flash** : $0.30 / $1.20 to


**$0.12 / $0.48** .


A dollar now buys two and a half times the tokens. And nobody had to wait for Black Friday.


**The fine print:** it’s OpenCode’s own hosted price, not the model makers’ price.


**Cut three: a solo developer, and the saving he refused.** Justin Ahinon runs WhatIsThatBook, which finds a book from a vague description. Finally, an app for “it had a blue cover, I think.” He shrank the prompt to about a third of its length (2,683 input tokens to 901), and moved it to a cheaper routing tier. The evening the routing change went live, his AI spend was about


**47%** lower than the evening before (


[Okupter](https://okupter.com/blog/reduce-llm-costs) ).


Then he tried something bigger: skip the model and search the catalog directly. That made a search almost free, about 99.96% cheaper. But the right book showed up in the top five only


**6%** of the time. Before, it was


**26%** . Technically, a book you never find is free. He didn’t ship it.


**The fine print:** one evening is not a month, in his own words. Part of the cost figure is an estimate. And the changes shipped late this summer.


The Department of Token Efficiency. Measure the result, not the receipt.
